newsitem.title: USA: U.S-N.Korea missile talks rescheduled for June.
newsitem.headline: U.S-N.Korea missile talks rescheduled for June.

text.p: U.S.-North Korean talks aimed at getting Pyongyang to halt its missile sales, postponed by North Korea earlier this month, have been rescheduled for mid-June, the State Department said on Tuesday.

The announcement followed other signs of renewed North Korean engagement with the outside world including an agreement on food aid from South Korea and an accord with the United States on missing U.S. servicemen from the Korean War.
State Department spokesman John Dinger said the missile talks would be held at the U.S. mission to the United Nations in New York June 11-13.
The talks were to have been held in New York May 12-13, but Pyongyang postponed them for what it called "technical reasons."
Dinger said the talks would be led for the United States by Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Robert Einhorn and for North Korea by Foreign Ministry Director Li Hyong-chol.
"We will address North Korea's missile proliferation activities, which are of great concern," he said.
The United States has made clear its concern over Pyongyang's missile sales to Iran and Syria and has said progress on this issue is crucial to improved U.S.-North Korean ties.
Previous talks on the issue were held in Berlin in April last year. "We hope to continue where we left off then," Dinger said.
Other U.S. concerns centre on reports, which have not been publicly confirmed, that North Korea may have deployed Rodong-1 ballistic missiles capable of hitting Japan.

News of the rescheduling of the missile talks came one day after the North and South Korean Red Cross societies signed an agreement under which Seoul will supply 50,000 metric tons of food aid to the hungry North by the end of July.

The deal, signed in Beijing, is the first since 1985 between the Red Cross societies of the two rival Koreas, and is part of international efforts to help the Stalinist North ward off a looming famine.

The United States has also sent limited aid. A first instalment, consisting of 27,000 metric tons of rice, corn and corn soy blend worth approximately $10 million, arrived in North Korea earlier this month.

A second instalment of 50,000 metric tons of corn valued at approximately $15 million, first announced on April 15, is expected to arrive in North Korea on two vessels on June 4 and June 26, Dinger said.
In another sign of improved ties, the United States and North Korea agreed on May 14 to conduct three new searches for remains of U.S. troops missing in North Korea since the 1950-53 Korean War.
They will also examine archives in Pyongyang for information on missing Americans.

The United States and South Korea, however, are still awaiting a definitive North Korean response on whether and when Pyongyang will attend proposed four-party peace talks on the future of the Korean peninsula.

North Korea has demanded large-scale food aid, a lifting of U.S. trade sanctions and diplomatic recognition as preconditions for entering such talks, which would be attended by the two Koreas, the United States and China.
Washington has said major food aid will have to await the opening of the talks, which would aim to replace the current armistice in Korea with a permanent peace treaty.
